In order to build resume and experience, I would recommend a few strategies:

1) Become proficient in R or Python. Unless you're an excellent programmer, your time will be better used by focusing solely on one language. For R, being familiar with Hadley Wickham's packages and the Rob Hyndman's forecast package goes a long way. Also, developing a Shiny app would be beneficial. For Python, knowing scikit-learn and the pandas package is useful. Working with iPython notebooks is recommended.

2) Become comfortable with cloud computing resources, e.g. Amazon Web Services (EC2, RDS, S3, RedShift, DynamoDB).

3) Be proficient with both a SQL data persistence solution (e.g., MySQL) and a NoSQL solution (e.g., MongoDB). Develop your own criteria of when each solution is appropriate to persist data.

4) Become great at retrieving and manipulating data (this may be accomplished via R or Python, or via *nix (Unix or Linux) command line tools (awk, sed, grep, etc.)).

5) For me, a Data Scientist is someone who uses the scientific method (develop testable hypotheses and subject them to rigorous analysis) and excellent (A) analytical skills or (B) development skills to take a project end-to-end. For (A) types, analysis is the end goal. End-to-end is: find data, retrieve data, organize data, explore data, analyze data, visualize analysis, and present findings. For (B) types, a data product (e.g., API) is the end goal. End-to-end is: find data, retrieve data, organize data, explore data, analyze data, develop algorithm, and 'package' output of algorithm.

6) Conduct your own analysis and/or data product, and share it with the world! Host your repositories on GitHub and be sure to demonstrate that you can take an analysis or data product from end-to-end.

Do you really have monthly seasonality? That would be very unusual, but it does sometimes happen. Much more common is both weekly and annual seasonality. Monthly seasonality would arise if you had end-of-month effects due to accounting practices, but I can't think of anything else that would cause them. I think you would need to consider what is causing the monthly seasonality and try to allow for it explicitly. It is not strictly seasonal as the periodicity is not regular.

Lots of good advice here already. I'd add:

1) Get an internship and demonstrate that you can fit into the corporate culture. Employers like to see that you can also complete assignments that you didn't select yourself, because those tend to be more interesting than the ones you are faced with in the Real World. Unfortunately, there is something of a chicken-and-egg problem there.

2) "Data science" is currently an ill-defined grab bag of things. I heartily second Rob's recommendation to use multiple search terms. Probably best to start with anything that contains the word "data" anywhere... Although you'll then be inundated with job postings for database administrators. To your student,

I quite understand how you feel at the moment. I had similar issues when I started looking for jobs after I graduated from my second PhD. All of the answers I got from potential employers was that "I did not have enough corporate experience." My degrees in Mathematics and Quantum Chemistry did not get me anywhere although I tried so hard to explain them that their job advertisement fits what I have done in my previous roles at university as a researcher.

I understand building up an impressive resume is important and previous comments give excellent directions but, honestly, no one has time for that. Everything that has been suggested requires time. And, when you are about to graduate, there is not enough time for anything.

So, what do you do? You learn the job at the job. Australia and New Zealand are famous for start up companies that are looking for interns/junior roles. If you have relevant experience, then it is all up to you how you "sell" yourself to the employer. The new culture that is emerging in these companies is very welcoming. All you have to do is be humble, be yourself and stay true to your word.

In my first interview, they asked if I had any experience with R, Pyhton, SQL, etc. I told them I had no experience in any of those things. I thought I failed. But, they invited me for the second interview. This time with the team leader. Again, I told him I had no experience in any of the latest technologies in data science and he replied with "I am not worried about any of those things. I am sure you are more than capable of learning and mastering those skills." Did I get the job? I did. I am currently employed as the Data Insights Analyst at a software development company. This was a year ago. Now, for example, I can write complex SQL scripts, design stored procedures for web apps, create dashboards, analyze complex time series and such.

So, don't be discouraged. You need to find the right people. And, trust me, you will find the right company to work for. Just be yourself.

P.S. Don't worry too much about all those weird looking names that has been suggested. If you need to use them, you will learn and use them.

I took Probability Theory with him in undergrad. There is no match at the statistics department who can teach like him. This guy was patient and calm. None of that, I teach you one thing in class but test you in something else; Or, everything on the test looks like the practice exam. He spends a quarter of the year teaching in the U.S. and then going back to Australia. The time adjustment cannot be good for his health. When he taught me in Probability class, I can tell he was always catching his breath between sentences at the podium. But, I didn't know he would die 5 years later. Another time he and I were both at a department seminar: the side pocket of my backpack was unzipped, there's really nothing expensive in there, a couple of pencils and an eraser. He would pause his conversation with the professors, walk over to my circle to let me know. I'm pretty sure not may professors in that room would do such a thing. Boy, I am at a loss hearing this, I wish I had known and given him better advice on health. Age 64 is way too young.

I went through this a couple years ago, although it was after an M.A. (in economics), not an undergrad degree. My strategy, which I continue to recommend to anyone who will listen, was to think of a career as something that's built incrementally. I looked for jobs with my particular skill set, with an opportunity to learn more data science-y stuff as part of the job. After a year at a tech company as a business intelligence developer with a stats bent, I was qualified to be a data scientist at Facebook (what I consider the gold standard for a sexy data science position). It took a lot of work, especially in my spare time, but I just kept making progress. For me, it took a masters, 1.5 years of job experience, and 4 years of self-study in stats and programming to be roughly qualified for my dream job (which isn't at FB, by the way).

As someone with an undergraduate degree, in a crowded job market, you may have to take something that's less than ideal. Frankly, entry level data science positions are few and far between. But as long as you're able to learn some data science on the job, you're moving in the right direction.

If I want to use a for loop like this and average the point forecasts of auto.arima and stlf methods - how would I need to change the code? I got as far as the modified for loop below, but it returns NA's for all the forecasts. Any ideas?

for(i in 1:ns)
fit5 <- stlf(retail[,i])
fcast[,i] <- forecast(fit5, h=h)$mean

Try this:

for(i in 1:ns)
{
fc1 <- forecast(stlf(retail[,i],h=h))
fc2 <- forecast(auto.arima(retail[,i]),h=h)
fcast[,i] <- 0.5*(fc1$mean + fc2$mean)
}
That worked perfectly! I did not think to set it up that way. I very much appreciate your help.

Looking at the forecast interval of ARIMA(0,0,0)+c (white noise with offset), I see that the prediction interval corresponds with the prediction interval of a normal distribution when assuming the mean and variance are known ànd equal to the sample mean and mle variance.

I am a bit puzzled by this result, as with forecasting, mean and variance are generally unknown. Is my conclusion correct that one gets more accurate results (ànd wider prediction intervals) by calculating the prediction interval by multiplying the (mle) variance by (n+1)/(n-1) (see e.g. https://en.wikipedia.org/wi... ) and then using the student's T distribution percentiles? Can one apply the same correction to other, more complex forecast models?

Adjusting the variance by multiplying by (n+1)/(n-1) is only valid in the very simple example discussed in the wiki article. Besides, it makes almost no difference.

Using a t-distribution would be better, but again it doesn't make much difference in practice.

The prediction intervals are too narrow for several reasons, as explained in this article. The t-distribution fix only corrects for the unknown variance, not for the parameter uncertainty, model uncertainty, etc.

For cross-validations for time series, in Step-2 do I need to use y(1),y(2),........y(m)? That would mean that I am using more inputs from past every time. Or, should I just use a fix length of inputs from y(t) to y(t-m)?

I've said nothing at all about inputs here. You are assuming some model.

The length of the training data is increasing with each iteration. In some circumstances, it is preferable to have a fixed window length for the training data.
If the length of training is increasing then this is not pure cross-validation, what is also getting taken into account is the so called auto-correlation part. Is that correct?

What is taken into account is that the past is used to predict the future, and not vice-versa. Accounting for autocorrelation is one feature of that, but not the only one. There are some circumstances when true cross-validation will work with time series data as explained in this paper: http://robjhyndman.com/work...

Hi there, Great post! Thanks. What are your opinions on when to use portmanteau versus LM tests both in AR and VAR processes?

They have very different purposes. A portmanteau test is checking whether residuals are white noise. LM tests are used for model selection. I never use LM tests myself as I think the AIC is a better approach.

Awesome post, thanks Rob!

I was asked to summarize in a couple of sentences what the tbats formula does.
Would you agree with the following summary?

1. Apply a Box-Cox transformation if Y is not normally distributed*
2. Model the seasonality with Fourier series **
3. Model the remaining auto-correlation, once the effect of seasonality has been removed, with an ARMA process **

* That's not a guarantee that Y will be normally distributed after the transformation.
** The parameters K for the Fourier series and (p,q) for the ARMA process are chosen by minimizing the AIC of the fitted model.

Thanks!

Not quite.

1. Y is not required to be normal, and usually won't be due to the trend and seasonality. Instead, the residuals are assumed normal with constant variance, and the BC transformation will normally allow that to occur.

2. The seasonality is modelled with Fourier-like terms that can change coefficients over time. Also, a local linear time trend is included, as it is in an ETS model.

3. Yes

All terms are selected by minimizing the AIC, not just the ARMA orders.

Hello Prof. Hyndman,

I went through the entire derivation of AIC. Two things that attracted my attention.

1) The derivation is based on unconditional distributions. The entropy of the true density is ignored with the assumption that it will be the same for all candidate models. It gets interesting once we try to apply AIC to conditional models like regression. At this point if the conditioning set is changing while keeping the target variable same, it gets fuzzy what true density we are talking about and which entropy is being ignored. This is related to point #6 above. Normally it is widely accepted that one can use AIC on nested models. But even in nested models the conditioning is changing.

2) The last step when TIC expression is simplified to AIC by taking the trace of a matrix, the only way that matrix becomes identity and trace becomes a simple dimension of the matrix is when the model is equivalent to truth. This makes AIC questionable when truth is not within the candidates.

What's your opinion?

It is a dated discussion, but, if you want an update, I just completed an undergraduate degree in economics -- with several econometrics course, including a graduate course in econometrics.

If you want an example of data driven choice, consider fitting a moving average model, an autoregressive model or a combination of both on a given time series. A quick ad hoc check you can do is look at correlograms (both partial and normal) knowing that the impulse response function of all three processes differ greatly -- e.g., MA process have a shorter memory whereas shocks reverbate for very long in AR processes. This obviously have implications for modeling from a statistical perspective, but also as far as economic theory is concerned: if you can well approximate the behavior of a time series with a moving average model, a theory that gets you long lasting effects and slow adjustment likely is wrong. So, correlograms is one way we often see what is going with macro and financial data.

Another usual plot we perform is a simple line plot of the time series -- does it look stationary? If it is too messy, we should bother to use unit root tests and make sure we work with stationary series. This is actually something we always do -- and if I pick a growth rate or a first difference, I also plot it to see if I get what I expect. Those plots can also reveal heteroskedasticity -- perhaps episodes of high and low variance, which may be well represented by ARCH processes.

We also usually pick ranges of lags with correlograms and formalize that argument with information criteria -- which also are data driven.

Remember that it is not because you do not see visual representations in seminars that no one used it. They might simply believe it is not sufficiently forceful or superfluous.

`Arima` and `auto.arima` will handle missing values. No need to impute them.

Yes, residuals should look like white noise. So no seasonalities.

With weekday data, your seasonalities will be 5 and 365.25*5/7. You *might* have a monthly seasonality as well if you have end-of-month accounting procedures, or some other activity on fixed days of the month. They are harder to account for as there are not 4 weeks in a month, and the months are not of equal length. Consequently, you might find it better to use dummy variables for the days in which such monthly activities occur.

The periodogram is not a good way to find seasonalities. If you must estimate them, use a smoothed spectral estimate. Better still, use your knowledge of the data without estimating the seasonal periods.

The Fourier terms are meant to handle the seasonality, so I generally do not include seasonal ARIMA components as well. It is possible that you need more Fourier terms if there is still seasonality that the ARIMA model is picking up. The trouble with MAPE is not only that it's asymmetric, but also that it may distort the evaluation by making a worse forecast appear better. An example:

A (Actual observations) = 100, 1000
Fa (Forecast A) = 200, 1100
Fb (Forecast B) = 100, 500

MAPE(A, Fa) = 55
MAPE(A, Fb) = 25

By MAPE alone, it seems that forecast B is better than forecast A. However, in most cases (load forecasting, sales forecasting), the real-life cost of a forecast error is proportional to the absolute value of the residual, and forecast A is actually much better.

If we adopt a different metric:

APE = 100 sum(|yt - yt^|)/sum(yt)

...it's an entirely different story:

APE(A, Fa) = 200 / 1100 = 18.1
APE(A, Fb) = 500 / 1100 = 45.5

Now, I'm calling it APE, but I don't really know how it's called - it's like WAPE without the weights (i.e. with all weights set to 1), so APE seems reasonable. It's simple and easy to intepret, scale-invariant, works fine with zeroes, values close to zero, and negative values too (if the denominator is changed to sum(|yt|)).

There's MASE, of course, but I'd hate to explain how MASE works to a client - I'd much rather go with APE. (For that purpose, I'd skip over RMSE too - if one manages to reduce RMSE by, say, 10%, how much will it save in the actual costs? Well, if the cost is more or less directly proportional to absolute error - and it typically is - then it's anyone's guess.)

A strange thing about MASE is that, if the observations are shuffled (i.e. if they occur in a different order), and the forecasts are rearranged accordingly, then MASE changes, possibly by a large margin. That seems somewhat counter-intuitive: if we have two forecasts with the same pairs of observations and predictions {yt, yt^}, only in a different order, then one would expect them to be evaluated as same (although, to be fair, this is really a theoretical rather than practical consideration).

I understand that when percentage (rather than absolute) errors are important, MAPE may be better - but in other cases (that's nine times out of ten, I'd say), why e.g. APE isn't more widely used? (In accuracy() too, perhaps?) Is there a reason to pick MASE over APE?

I'm wondering the same thing when comparing with SAS and with another blog post (which I see you had commented on).

The SAS equation is show on the last line here: http://support.sas.com/docu....

The blog post is:
http://davegiles.blogspot.c...

But one thing to note is that their sigma is the sigma of the transformed variable I think. When I've dug into the forecast package source code and recreated the result it seems to be using the sigma on the untransformed residuals:

fittedVariance <- model$residuals %>% var

fcMean <- fcMedian * (1 + 0.5 * fittedVariance)

I think the issue here is to do with approximations vs exact results. Note that exp(a) is approximately 1+a when a is small. So exp(mu + sigma^2/2) is approximately exp(mu)[1+sigma^2/2] provided sigma^2 is small. My Taylor series approximation is a convenient approximation that works pretty well in many situations. The problem is that checking stationarity of x only makes sense when x is random, and there is no way for auto.arima to tell whether x is fixed or random. The user needs to take some responsibility here. An automated procedure cannot determine the context of the data. Checking the residuals of y~x is a bare minimum test -- if either y or x is non-stationary, and they are not cointegrated, then the residuals will be non-stationary.

Statistical modelling requires careful thinking, and an awareness of the robustness of the results to the model choices made. You can't just blindly follow recipes or automated procedures.

I was studying out-of-sample one-step forecasts, but then I realized I had a doubt with in-sample forecasts. I arrive at the same fitted (one-step in-sample forecasts) when I (i) fit the model for the whole sample and then use fitted() and; (ii) when I split the sample into two, use the coefficients of the model estimated with the whole sample to forecast the "training set" adding one obs. each time in a loop. This is exactly what I expected.

However, when I try a third "test" I arrive at an odd result (at least to me...). Now, I use the coefficients estimated with the whole sample to fit only the "test set". As I used the same coeffcients in the three cases, I expected to find the same fitted results here too, but that's not the case... Let me show you the script.

Thanks in advance!

library(forecast)
data("gas")

#Model fitted with the whole sample
model <- auto.arima(gas)

#Definitions for forecasting
h <- 1 #prediction horizon
start <- start(gas) #Series start
train_end <- c(1990,12) #End of the training period
series_end <- end(gas) #End of the series
n <- length(gas-window(gas, end=train_end)) - h + 1 #Quantity of months tested
a <- (c(1995,12)-series_end+c(0,1))[2] #Months till the end of the year
#Creating the training dates for the loop
test_date <- matrix(NA, nrow=12*(end(gas)[1]-train_end[1])+1, ncol=2)
test_date[1,1:2] <- c(1990,12)
test_date[2:nrow(test_date),1] <- rep((train_end[1]+1):end(gas)[1],each=12)
test_date[2:nrow(test_date),2] <- rep(1:12, end(gas)[1]-train_end[1])

## FIRST WAY OF ESTIMATING ONE-STEP-AHEAD IN-SAMPLE FORECASTS
# Use the fitted values of the estimated model from the whole sample
model1 <- Arima(gas, model=model)

fc1 <- window(fitted(model1), start=train_end+c(1,-11))

## SECOND WAY OF ESTIMATING ONE-STEP-AHEAD IN-SAMPLE FORECASTS
# Use the estimated model in a loop, adding one observation each period

#matrix that will store the forecasts
fc2 <- ts(matrix(0, nrow=n, ncol=h), start=train_end+c(1,-11), end=series_end, freq=12)

#Loop to calculate the forecasts
for(i in 1:(nrow(test_date)-a))
{
fc2[i] <- forecast(Arima(window(gas, end=test_date[i,], freq=12), model=model), h=h)$mean
}

## THIRD WAY OF ESTIMATING ONE-STEP-AHEAD IN-SAMPLE FORECASTS
# Use the fitted values of the estimated model only in the testing period (from c(1995,12) on)
model3 <- Arima(window(gas, start=train_end+c(1,-11)), model=model)

fc3 <- fitted(model3)

#COMPARING THE THREE RESULTS
View(cbind(fc1, fc2,fc3))

1. include.constant is more general. It will include a constant in any Arima model, include.drift is only relevant when d=1. include.drift is retained for backwards compatibility.

2. You can handle a linear trend by including a time covariate via xreg.

3. The time trend becomes a constant after differencing, it is not removed.

4. If the AR polynomial has no unit root, then you don't have a drift term -- you have a linear trend.

If the AR polynomial does have a unit root of order d, then you actually have a forecast function in the form of a polynomial of order d+1.

In neither case do you have a simple drift term.

Well, although you are correct that one of intervals you describe is often times referred to as a "prediction interval," it is wrong to tell your students and request correction of the paper you referee if they refer to it as a "confidence interval," for prediction intervals are indeed confidence interval, in which the object of interest is the realization of a random variable. For instance, Maddala (1992, p. 87) never defines the term prediction interval, as he refers to what you call prediction interval as a "confidence interval." In summary, all prediction intervals are confidence intervals but not all confidence intervals are prediction intervals and that's the only distinction to be made.

Reference:
Maddala, G. S. (1992). Introduction to Econometrics (2nd ed.). New York, NY: Macmillan.

Seasons of length 300+ are not really "long": e.g. taylor dataset ("Half-hourly electricity demand") has a season of length 336 (48 obs/day x 7 days in a week), and 168 (24 x 7) is also very common in load forecasting.

I could not make auto.arima() work for taylor dataset at all, even when I downsampled it to 24 obs/day, which sadly meant that ARIMA was useless for load forecasting in general (weekly seasonality is rather strong, so simply using daily seasons of length 24 as a workaround is bound to produce poor models). Fortunately, now (R 3.3.3 - haven't tried 3.4.0 yet) I'm unable to reproduce this behavior, so perhaps it's no longer a problem.

Still, my advice for load forecasters would be: don't forget to try dshw(), it's super robust and performs surprisingly well.

Here is an everyday example of a time series with monthly seasonality: ATM usage (i.e. the amount of money withdrawn per day). In practice, usage peaks tend to correspond to dates when salaries and pensions are paid, as well as dates when various utility bills are due (phone, electricity, etc.). Since these dates are usually fixed (e.g. 10th day of every month), a monthly pattern is easily observed.

To make matters worse, in this particular example it is obvious that there's weekly seasonality too. So, on top of the usual problems with months not being the same length, there is also a problem of the longer season generally not being a multiple of the shorter season.

ATM usage - as described above - is virtually impossible to model as a time series. Indeed, the best way is to use regressor variables. Lagged variables (usage one month ago, usage one week ago) might be useful too.

1. Mean added so the adjusted data has same level as original data. Otherwise it would have mean close to 0.
2. Let r = 1 minus the ratio of variances (as explained in the paper). If r<0, it returns 0. If r>1, it returns 1. Otherwise it returns r.
Apologies for not being clear in my question. I understand the math you mentioned in point 2. I am struggling to understand the reason for this math to be a measure of trend (strength)? Thanks!

x=Trend+Seasonal+Remainder.

Adjusted = x-Trend-Seasonal=Remainder.

Deseason = x-Seasonal = Trend+Remainder

So V(adjusted) includes only remainder variation while V(Deseason) includes both remainder variation and trend variation. Hence V(adjusted)/V(Deseason) will be small if trend variation is high, but large (close to 1) if there is essentially no trend.

I still think that flat a forecast by arima is, in a sense, bug.

Consider the following test-code:
If you left "0.8*x[i-24]" commented, you get an Arima without a seasonal component and the forecast is very flat.
If you uncomment it, there is 24-periodicity and the forecast seems much more plausible (it flattens quick but not immediately).

That's why in practice I sometimes use STL even for non-seasonal and non-trendy models.
The forecasts made by STL are theoretically invalid but in practice are better than from ARIMA.

x = rnorm(1008, 0,1)
y = array(0.0, dim=1008)
y[1] = x[1]
for(i in 25:1008)
{
y[i] = 0.6*y[i-1] + x[i] #uncomment it to get periodicity+ 0.8*x[i-24]
}
par(mfrow=c(1,2))

auto.arima(y) #retuns unfeasable results
armaMod = Arima(y, order=c(1,0,0), seasonal=list(order=c(1,0,0), period=24)) #much better
prog = forecast(armaMod, 100)
plot(prog)

stlMod = stl(ts(y, frequency=24), s.windo="period")
#plot(stlMod)
prog = forecast(stlMod, 100, method="arima")
plot(prog)

Is it common to see Ljung Box test (p value) suggesting 'the residuals of a ARIMA model is not auto correlated' while the correlogram (ACF/PACF) of the residuals do show some significant autocorrelations?
In such cases how reasonable will it be to rely on the Ljung Box test result and ignore the results from correlogram, or we should consider the ACF/PACF plots equally important?

The LB test is a test on several autocorrelations. You might have one just outside the limits, but the rest well inside, so as a group they are not significant. You can also have many autocorrelations close to the critical values, but none beyond them, but as a group they are significant.

I suggest that comparing run-times without verifying *effectively equal output* is perhaps hasty. By "effective", I mean disregarding things such as unrelated attributes introduced by `tibble`, `group_by`, etc. As one comment suggested, `d1()` is not equal to the others: it is only unique-ifying by one column, not four, so its work is significantly less. So either add the additional columns to `d1` or dumb-down the remaining three.

Additionally, you could remove ancillary functions that are not enabling anything: `as_tibble`, `select`, and even the `%>%` operator (which does add an ever-so-slight measurable overhead):

The results are not significantly different, once `d1` is adjusted to ensure `identical` results. (Please disregard my omission of braces, admittedly another possible overhead but I'm discarding it for brevity.)


d1 <- function() unique(faraway::psid[c('person','sex','educ','age')])
d5 <- function() faraway::psid %>% as_tibble() %>% distinct(person, sex, educ, age)
d6 <- function() faraway::psid %>% distinct(person, sex, educ, age)
d7 <- function() distinct(faraway::psid, person, sex, educ, age)
microbenchmark(d1(), d2(), d3(), d4(), d5(), d6(), d7(), times=100)
# Unit: milliseconds
#  expr       min        lq      mean    median        uq       max neval
#  d1()  1.617688  1.773950  2.003771  1.841050  1.992206  4.148880   100

#  d3() 12.426583 13.132042 14.839268 13.762014 15.735075 37.094859   100
#  d4()  9.743687 10.374571 11.207165 10.828588 11.423551 18.804342   100
#  d5()  3.223706  3.461837  3.781425  3.614452  3.844014  6.094044   100
#  d6()  2.453518  2.696754  3.040578  2.802144  3.018031  6.634125   100
#  d7()  2.302543  2.532834  2.862560  2.663933  2.847729  5.559799   100

Hi Rob

Reading the interviews with the competition winner(s), I can see how, by focusing on outliers, one can make a forecast tool look very good. So do you now recommend Median Absolute Scaled Error or a Trimmed Mean Absolute Scaled Error?

I recommend tuning your forecasts according to how they will be judged. If MASE is being used, then optimize MASE when selecting and estimating the forecasting model. But if MSE is being used, then optimize MSE when selecting and estimating the model.

Thank you. I was thinking about this comment in particular:

"The MASE can be very sensitive to a few series, and to optimize MASE it is worth concentrating on these. (This is actually not a good message for forecasting overall, as we want good forecasts for all series. Maybe we need to find a metric with similar properties to MASE but with a less skewed distribution.)"

Do you still recommend MASE as a general purpose forecast accuracy metric or would something like Trimmed Mean ASE or Median ASE be preferred?

I haven't come up with anything better than MASE overall. I sometimes use MSSE (mean scaled squared errors) which have the added advantage of being optimal for the mean, but they are also very skewed. I don't like Median or trimmed means in this context as they ignore the series with the worse forecasts, and that is usually where you need to focus your attention.
Thank you for the insight!

Does anyone know what is the best approach to forecast with rolling mean, but returning a forecast object? I wrote the following function that can return a timeseries object using rollmean function, but I cannot convert it to forecast object. (the code is probably ugly because I am learning R)

forecast_mm_ <- function(y, h=52, meanfunction=rollmean, window=5) {
y <- as.ts(y)
n <- length(y)
f <- y*NA
freq <- frequency(y)

# first prediction considers h and window
first <- max(window, h)+1
fc <- try(suppressWarnings(meanfunction(y, k=window, na.pad=TRUE, align='right')), silent=TRUE)
f[first:n] <- fc[window:(length(fc)-h-1)]

# expand to new periods
for (i in 1:h) {
f <- c(f, mean( f[(length(f)-window+1):length(f)] ))
}
f <- (f[(length(f)-h+1):length(f)])

# msts object
newStart <- end(y)
newStart[2] <- newStart[2]+1
if (newStart[2] > freq) {
newStart[2] <- 1
newStart[1] <- newStart[1]+1
}
return(ts(f, start=newStart, frequency=freq))
}

The S matrix does not have to be 0s and 1s. It can contain any linear constraints. So if you can write the problem as y = S b where b contains the component time series, and S contains the linear combinations, and y is all the time series, then you can use the same approach as we use for hierarchical reconciliation.

Le y_t = beta_1*x_t + beta_2* x_{t-1} + eta_t where eta ~ ARIMA(0,1,1).
If x_{t-1} is held fixed, and x_t goes up by 1, then y_t goes up by beta_1. If you difference the equation, you see the same thing:
y_t = y_{t-1} + beta_1(x_t-x_{t-1}) + beta_2(x_{t-1}-x_{t-2}) + theta e_{t-1} + e_t.
So if x_t goes up by 1, and y_{t-1}, x_{t-1} and x_{t-2} are unchanged, then y_t goes up by beta_1.

Interesting. No I wasn't aware of that.

They aren't really doing the same thing. Yours is about representation, mine is exclusively on univariate features. You can think of features as a type of representation I guess, and aspects of a representation might constitute features, so there is overlap. But I think they are sufficiently different that they can live in parallel. If your feature extraction functions return a simple numeric vector given a univariate ts input, then they can be used directly in tsfeatures. Otherwise, they might need wrapper functions.

"
Although a valid point, this would have excluded more than 95% of the methods (including ML and those based on exponential smoothing) that cannot produce prediction intervals, not to mention “full distribution forecasts”
"

ML methods that solve for quantiles can produce such distribution forecasts. While not all methods support quantiles, quite a lot of off the shelf implementations do, particularly boosted trees used pervasively in Kaggle (e.g. gbm, xgboost, lightGbm). They were used to win exactly such a task in GEFCom2014 (wind, 1st & 2nd). It is worth mentioning that directly solving for them in this way is different than the NNETAR prediction interval method mentioned in the follow-up.

However, I do agree that the additional complexity of generating such distributions will discourage those that are unsure about entering. Making it optional then adds a time-consuming task for those competing, so I think it unlikely that many will opt to submit those intervals. Especially if the evaluation metrics chosen are misaligned with distribution evaluation--the participant will have little incentive to add code and processing time to generate those. I'd argue that solving directly for them will provide proper evidence that the best methodology has been chosen for such a purpose. Those that provide them because they come "free" with the method chosen, have likely not optimized for them, and it would be difficult to conclude much with such a potential bias.

In any case, it still looks like an exciting competition! Thanks for your efforts in setting it up and encouraging participation.

if(!is.null(xreg))
{
# Make sure it is a matrix with column names
nmxreg <- deparse(substitute(xreg))
xregg <- as.matrix(xreg)
if(ncol(xregg)==1 & length(nmxreg) > 1)
nmxreg <- "xreg"
if (is.null(colnames(xregg)))
colnames(xregg) <- if (ncol(xregg) == 1) nmxreg
else paste(nmxreg, 1:ncol(xregg), sep = "")

# Check that xreg is not rank deficient
# First check if any columns are constant
constant_columns <- apply(xregg, 2, is.constant)
if(any(constant_columns)) # Remove first one
xregg <- xregg[,-which(constant_columns)[1]]

# Now check if it is rank deficient
sv <- svd(na.omit(cbind(rep(1,NROW(xregg)), xregg)))$d
if(min(sv)/sum(sv) < .Machine$double.eps)
stop("xreg is rank deficient")

# Finally find residuals from regression in order
# to estimate appropriate level of differencing
j <- !is.na(x) & !is.na(rowSums(xregg))
xx <- x
xx[j] <- residuals(lm(x ~ xregg))
}

Is the asymptotic equivalence of AIC and BIC with CV of any practical use? In my day to day work, I deal with a software package which is considered an industry standard in retail demand forecasting, and per their documentation - the automated model fitting process doesn't bother with test sets, it just fits different models to the training data and then chooses the model with the lowest BIC. Are they relying on the asymptotic BIC/CV equivalence? Or could there be another reason for this?

It is much more efficient to use AIC/BIC then to use test sets or CV, and it becomes essential for short time series where there is not enough data to do otherwise. The BIC is sometimes preferred over the AIC due to its consistency properties, but see https://robjhyndman.com/hyn... for my take on that.

Hello Rob:

RElated to you last sentence: The auto.arima function is even stricter and will not select a model with roots close to the unit circle either, as such models are unlikely to be good for forecasting.

Quite often, the estimation process provides as an optimal model one that has a unit root in the seasonal MA polynomial. If the model has a seasonal difference, the model is unstable to make predictions. What we do is manually correct the parameters of the seasonal polynomial, to put all of its zeros within the unit circle. Could you recommend me some elegant way to do this?

Thanks

J Juan
No. If there is a disagreement between the tests, you have to decide which one to use. And then what is the point of using both?
Can you please provide a reproducible example of the problem.

Thanks for your interest. I'll tell you more about the problem. We estimate 24 models ARIMA (0,1,3) x (0,1,2) _7, with the seasonal part equal to 7. Each model corresponds to one hour of the day. The variable is hourly electricity demand. In some of the 24 models (sometimes), the seasonal MA polynomial presents a unit root. The simplified model, ARIMA (0,1,3) x (0,0,2) _7 or ARIMA (0,1,3) x (0,0,1) _7 is clearly worse. However, the ARIMA (0,1,3) x (0,1,2) _7 model with unitary root is very unstable and sporadically gives very bad predictions.

The estimation and prediction system implemented is automatic and we would like the 24 models to have the same structure. We have empirical evidence that the best model is the ARIMA model (0,1,3) x (0,1,2) _7, but in some system, unit roots sometimes appear as those discussed above.

Provisionally, the solution implemented has been to slightly change the coefficients of the seasonal MA polynomial, to avoid the unit root. That solves the problem (for now). I would like to know your opinion about it and if there is any other way to correct this problem.

The system is programmed in MATLAB and includes meteorological variables (radiation, temperature) and other variables 0-1 to manage the holidays. It is used to make predictions of 13 different electrical systems. It is not easy to reproduce the problem in R.

What auto.arima does is to reject any model where the roots are within 0.01 of the unit circle. That avoids any problems with near unit roots. Also, a model with two terms that almost cancel will always be rejected because it will have a higher AIC value. I would never manually alter coefficients.

Thank you for your reply. The point of using both test simultaneously is outlined in many articles and books about econometry published in Czech Republic. One author in particular, Cipra (ISBN: 978-80-86929-93-4), states that only a time series which is proclaimed as either stationary or not stationary by both tests is reliably stationary. If one test implies stationaritry and the other does not, then the stationarity is inconclusive.

I know this is rather old now. But, I wanted to add at least one comment.

I am in a rather rigorous MA program that’s a “stepping stone” program to PhDs. During my studies, I have found that while economists due typically use robust to refer to heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation, I think this is just a common case of what they really mean. Throughout Wooldridge, he will refer to sandwich estimators as being “robust variance matrix estimators” or “robust inference.” What he means is these variance estimators (and statistical inference made using them) don’t require any second-moment assumptions of error terms, and are thus robust to model mispecification. And this what economists mean when they use robust: that an estimator is insensitive to model misspecification. It’s just the context when used is more often than not with standard errors due to the nature of economic data. Similarly, this is also how it’s used when talking about the efficiency vs robustness trade off. Estimators that are more effectient (MLE, FGLS, etc) are typically more sensitive to model mispecification.

One way to obtain future predictions is to run Opera and get the last weights returned by the model.
Run your different forecast methods and obtain future predictions.
Multiply the prediction of each forecast method with the weight returned by Opera.
Try this approach and check the results.
This is because Opera is giving weights (ratios) to different forecasting methods based on their prediction accuracy compared to the test sample.
Check the github page with its example: https://github.com/dralliag...

I'd like to draw your attention to KDD Cup 2018 as well. Since 1997, KDD Cup has been a prestigious annual data mining competition organized by ACM SIGKDD.

KDD Cup 2018 is a timeseries competition, where participants are asked to predict air pollution levels over the coming 48 hours for two cities, Beijing, China, and London, UK.

Unlike previous timeseries competitions, we provide the real time data API, and during the test phase (5/2018), everyday participants need to pull new data, generate 48 hour forecast, and submit it for evaluation.

We hope that this setup addresses some of major critics/problems on previous competitions such as:
* Winning solutions that are too complex: Since teams need to train their models everyday with new data, it cannot be too complex.
* Data leakage for the test data: Since the test data set is strictly from the future, there cannot be leakage.
* Metrics that are not aligned with real world use cases: The setup mimics the forecasting pipeline in practice (not one time forecasting, but continuous forecasting over time with new data).

Please check out the KDD Cup 2018 website for more information: https://biendata.com/compet...

Jeong

Hello Prof. Hyndman. When estimating a model to do direct multiperiod forcesasts of horizon h do you take all samples or every h sample? The reason I am asking is if we use all samples the residuals end up autocorrelated. This breaks standard t-stats. If I don't care about the t-stats is it better to use all samples for the sake of better prediction? Also does this autocorrelation in residuals affect the k-fold cross validation procedure? Thank you

All data should be used to give better estimates. But yes, the residuals will be autocorrelated. Our theory for k-fold CV is based on one-step forecasting for estimation, and recursive forecasting for multi-step. When you estimate multi-step models, I think the CV theory may break down due to the autocorrelations that will be induced.

I think this is simply those data-mining researchers who want to "specify" the word "prediction" in their "discipline". I would say that it's a matter of choosing a tool for making an equation for "prediction". This tool can be either statistical inference (deductive reasoning approach) or predictive modeling (inductive reasoning approach). When I learned knowledge management, I came across the statement: Without true facts, we may induce false models. The typical example is about the swans in Europe being all white. But, this rule is wrong in Australia that has swans with black color. Prediction based on predictive modeling may be wrong due to the non-representative sample. In contrast, it is not to say that statistical inference "must" draw adequate prediction, which depends on what variables are selected to predict. However, as I mentioned before, it is a matter of choice between the two tools for making a prediction equation. I personally don't think that prediction can only be associated with predictive modeling.

Hi Rob, For test purposes, if I wanted to get a baseline of “correct” D values, run auto.arima with D=0, then rerun with D=1. Evaluate MASE for both. Baseline D value is the one with lowest MASE.

Then for evaluating methods use percent agreement to baseline?

Edit: or would tsCV be a better diagnostic to determine which D is “correct”?
No particular reason. Either works for our purposes as one is a linear transformation of the other. Spectral entropy is better known, but Omega might be more interpretable as you point out.

Assuming you mean in-sample MASE, the issue will be the two models could have different degrees of freedom and then MASE values are not comparable in-sample. If you meant out-of-sample MASE, there usually won't be enough data to draw any meaningful conclusion about D on a single data set. Instead, we use a measure of seasonal strength on the whole data set, and choose the threshold based on applying the measure to the M3 time series. That way we get to use a lot of data to decide where to draw the line.

tsCV could work here but would be very time consuming. Also, you would need to be careful in computing MSE of cross-validated errors to make sure you only used values which were non-missing on both D=0 and D=1.

I'm trying to estimate ARIMA+Fourier. I have non-stationary data, so auto.arima provides the result in first differences ARIMA(1,1,2) + S1-7 and C1-7 coefficients(I took k = 1 just for simplicity in order to check it manually). I made calculation like this:
h = 1, ARIMA(1,1,2) + Fourier
y_{t+1) = y_{t}*(1+\phi_1) - \phi_1*y_{t-1} + e_{t+1} +\theta_1*e_{t} + \theta_2*e_{t-1} + \alpha*sin(2pi*1*(t+1)/7) + \beta*cos(2*pi*1*(t+1)) , where
\phi_1 - coeff AR(1) from R
\theta_1, \theta_2 - coeff MA(1), MA(2) from R
e_{t+1} = 0
\alpha and \beta are coeff S1-7 and C1-7
So, using the formula above I calculated a forecasted value h = 1 that was different from the value of R forecast(). I think that the alleged asymmetry of the MAPE pointed out by Armstrong is a false problem. MAPE #is# symmetric, since it equally penalizes underestimation and overestimation; that is, if $y_{t}=150$, then a prediction of $\hat{y}_{t}=100$ and a prediction of $\hat{y}_{t}=200$ will be equally penalized by MAPE, and this is (I think) good. The unintuitive aspect in Armstrong’s thinking (and throughout this blog post) is IMHO the idea that one should strive for a measure in which $y_{t}$ and $\hat{y}_{t}$ are interchangeable. But I do not see why this should be desirable: in prediction, the reference should always be the true value, and MAPE correctly considers it as the reference (the gold standard) by putting it at the denominator. True value and predicted value simply do not have the same status. If I am allowed an analogy, true value is “the law” which individual behaviours should comply with, and you want to evaluate individual behaviours in terms of whether and how they comply with the law: you don’t evaluate how the law complies with individual behaviours, you simply don’t care.

A measure for evaluating the accuracy of prediction should be such that that it can fairly compare two different predictors that attempt to predict the same true value. Most if not all the measures that are mentioned in this post as being proposed to “amend” MAPE look unsuitable to me from this point of view; a suitable measure should equally penalize $\hat{y}_{t}=100$ and $\hat{y}_{t}=200$ when $y_{t}=150$, and none of these measures (aside MAPE) seem to do this. The only symmetry we should care about when measuring prediction accuracy is the one between underestimation and overestimation, which is (in the absence of prescriptions to the contrary) desirable.

Hi Professor,

Is it ever necessary to use time series CV to perform hyperparameter tuning for classical time series method such as ARIMA, ETS, or STL? From what it sounds like in this article tsCV() is used to find the true estimation of forecasting error alone right?
You can use CV to select the ARIMA order, or the ETS structure, or the STL windows. But for ARIMA and ETS, using the AIC is much more efficient.

The forecasts will probably be identical. But fable has much better facilities for handling the data. Yes, it can handle multi-seasonality and there is no need to use msts objects with fable. Rather than translate the msts to tsibble, it is better to set up a proper date index.

Something that I noted when updating and running some older scripts.

When using auto.arima() with the xreg argument I had previously had my xregs in a data frame. Now, it insists I put them in a matrix. That isn't explicitly outlined in these notes and I was wondering if it was an unintended effect of reworking those few things.

Hasn't really caused me any serious issues, I've just been applying as.matrix() to my old xreg data frames. Still, it'd be nice if the code ran as it use to. Also wondering if the need to have factors in my xreg "data frame" will cause issues later on.

This is because xreg should be numeric, and factors in data frames would silently be translated to numbers giving inappropriate coefficients as a result. So we made it return an error for a data frame so that users must coerce it to be a numerical matrix.

The fable package will handle factors in an ARIMA model via a formula interface, just like lm does.
Yes, it would be easy enough to write a simulate method for linear models. We just haven't done it.

Hi Rob, a question from an old discussion about stl decomposition forecasting. In train/test, is it cheating to include all of the train+test data in the decomposition to get the seasonal component used in the test phase, or must you use the naive seasonal forecast? My thoughts are, if you are comparing various ets/arima models within STL it's ok, but if you are comparing STL to other methods it's not ok. Curious to hear your opinion.

Thanks!

By using the estimated seasonal component, you are removing a source of variation in the comparisons. If the alternative is to use the same estimate of the seasonal component in the comparisons (e.g., when comparing ets/arima after decomposition) it probably doesn't matter much. But if the comparisons also involve estimating the seasonal component in the future using different methods (e.g., compare full ets vs ets after decomposition) then only the training data should be used.

Can one generalize that LB is more suited for use with ARIMA models?

No. It is a test for correlated residuals. But failing the test does not necessarily mean that (a) the model produces poor forecasts; or (b) that the prediction intervals are in accurate. It suggests that there is a little more information in the data than is captured in the model. But it might not matter much.

In the msts() function, use seasonal.periods = c(7, 365.25); then, carry out decomposition using mstl(). if you have insufficient data to work with annual seasonality, the plots would tell you. Then, the only option you're left with is weekly seasonality, i.e. 7. It's important to assess the possible seasonalities for high frequency data; however, not all will be relevant to your objective. In that case, set ts.frequency in msts() to the seasonality that is most important to your objective. Don't be too reliant on tests as they are susceptible to type I and II errors. If your data have seasonality, then the time series is non-stationary; check the ACF plots to have a better understanding. There will be spikes at seasonal lags if the data have seasonality. It is also possible to misinterpret cyclic behavior as seasonal; however if data are cyclic, then it would be stationary as cyclic patterns are of fixed duration and are not periodic, making the mean constant over a period of time. Hope this helps!

Hi,
It's a matter of understanding of what can be the periodic patterns when you have data with different frequencies (daily, hourly, quarterly, etc.). For instance, assume you have daily data of sales of a restaurant. You would observe that during weekends, the sales shoot up; this can be attributed to the fact that on weekends families and friends go out, resulting in increased sales.This pattern would repeat every week, and hence, we say your daily data has weekly seasonality of 7. However, if specify any integer when you declare your data as ts() or msts(), you would observe periodic patterns when the data is decomposed. However, integers other than 7 would be difficult to explain when you present your results as they are non-standard. Going forward, the restaurant may also see increased sales during a given time of the year, for instance, Christmas to New Year. This would repeat every year and hence, you can expect yearly seasonality too in daily data. So, when you create time series, the seasonality that you specify largely follows from your understanding of how the data behave. For convenience, researchers have already made it easy for us to pick seasonality based on the type of data we have. Just choose the possible seasonality(s) based on the type of data you have; if you want to reason why this is the case, analyse (the example I quoted is one such case, there can be many). ACF plots help you understand if your data have trend, or seasonality, or both. If your data is trended, then the the spikes in ACF plots would decrease gradually as the observations would have strong correlations with their neighbors. If your data is seasonal, you would observe significant spikes at seasonal lags while other spikes wouldn't be significant. If your data is both trended and seasonal, you would see a scalloped shape in you ACF as your data would not only gradually decreasing spikes as lags progress but also significant spikes at seasonal lags. PACF removes the effect of intermediate observations between two observations when you want to understand the correlation between two specific observations; this is because in ACF plots, intermediate observations also have am effect on the correlation between two specific observations of interest. Hope this helps.

Hi,
Daily data have essentially weekly seasonality and/or yearly seasonality. You don't have to specify all of them, just mention the ones that are relevant to your business objective.
Check for residuals and see if they represent white noise. If not, you may want to look at regression with arima errors. Such a model initially fits a regression model and then an arima model on the residuals from the regression model. The mean forecast is a combination of forecasts from regression and arima parts. Such a model improves the confidence interval as the residuals are likely to be white noise or close to it. You can also look at NNs. Also, avoid random sampling of data into training and test as time series data have a chronological order and random sampling may lead to loss of time series dynamics. There are a lot of approaches to adopt, a bit of reading might help. Hope this helps.

mod1.fcst2 knows nothing about the data prior to the first observation of x2, whereas mod1.fcst1 can compute forecasts based on that data. So mod1.fcst1 gives forecasts conditional on the data, whereas mod1.fcst2 gives forecasts unconditional on the data, even though they both use the same model.

Are we talking about the same thing? I (a) fit the model to training data; (b) use fitted(Arima(test, model = cafe.train)) to get one-ahead-errors on test; then (c) alter the last value of test and re-run step (b). Steps (b) and (c) are the same call, using the same model, only the last value of test (and resulting output) differs. I am not asking about using the forecast function.

Fitted values are one-step forecasts. A fitted value at time t requires knowledge of the model, its parameters, and any historical data up to and including time t-1. When you pass a model to fitted, you are giving it the model order and the parameters. You are not providing the historical data. So fitted() applied to a test set does not use data from the training set, it only uses the model and its parameters.

"A fitted value at time t requires knowledge of the model, its parameters, and any historical data up to and including time t-1."
In the example I posted a couple of days ago (the cafe data from section 12.8 of your book), the only thing I changed between successive calls to fitted(Arima(test, model = cafe.train)) was the last value of test (i.e. the observed value at time t). The subsequent output of this call (i.e., one-step forecasts) had a different (fitted) value for time t. To me this appears to indicate that fitted() is also pulling information from the test value at time t, since nothing else (model, parameters, historical data up to and including time t-1) changed.

When there is no differencing, c=μ(1−ϕ1−⋯−ϕp) and μ = an estimate of the mean of the training data. When there is a drift term (with d=1 and D=0), the drift parameter is μ and estimate of the mean of the first differenced data. Note that the estimate of the mean in each case is not necessarily the sample mean.

The drift term induces a linear trend in the forecasts.

See https://otexts.com/fpp2/ari... for more details.

Hi Rob, well explained definitions, Thanks.
However, I think the second sentence from cyclic definition (i.e. *The duration of these fluctuations is usually of at least 2 years.*) should be removed.

I think, the difference between seasonal and cyclical behavior has nothing to do with the time scale. A seasonal behavior is very strictly regular, meaning there is a precise amount of time between the peaks and troughs of the data. Let's say temperature has a seasonal behavior. The coldest day of the year and the warmest day of the year may move but you will never see drift over time where eventually winter comes in June in the northern hemisphere.

Cyclical behavior on the other hand can drift over time because the time between periods **isn't precise**. For instance, the stock market tends to cycle between periods of high and low values, but there is no set amount of time between those fluctuations.

min_cases) %>% dplyr::mutate(edate = as.numeric(.data$date -

I am not sure I understand what you mean by 'data driven' model and how this is different (in your view) from 'model driven' model?

To my knowledge, the models used by the experts are statistical models, and their parameters are estimated based on the available data. Hence, they (IMHO) are 'data driven' models. And they have the same property as all models: they are only a (simplified) representation of reality, they are not reality itself.

You might also be overestimating the quality of the available data, or put differently underestimating the large variability in the collected data due to differences in the way the different countries/states measure (availability of testing kits, scope of testing, counting policies applied, ...). This variability does not mean the data cannot be used, it only means there is a large uncertainty around those estimates, and hence large uncertainty in the 'predictions' coming out of those models.

If you want to use the term 'guestimates' in this context, feel free, but I think you are then missing the point of why we use data, statistics and models in the first place.

I admire your faith in time series 😉

But the fact remains the data is inaccurate.

You may have suspicions as to why it is inaccurate, and theoretically you could turn those into some assumptions and use these to compensate the inaccurateness.
But... you have essentially no practical way to test your suspicions / assumptions... In other words, you still don't know if you can trust what your model comes up with, let alone base any conclusions on that.

BTW, from what I can see it is not just 'some countries manipulating the numbers' or 'under developed countries not testing enough'.
- There is no long-term historic data, only data of the past few weeks
- Testing falls short in all countries, not surprising the scale of testing that is needed, the shortage of resources, ...
- Different countries allocate the limited testing resources they have according to different priorities (for whatever good or bad reason they may have), these priorities change from one moment to the next
- Counting & reporting criteria (eg what is a Covid19 related death, what is not) are very different from country to country, the criteria also change on a moment's notice
- Delays in consolidation of within-country counts are different from country to country due to several country-specific factors
- The mitigation strategies / actions differ among countries, resulting in different effects on spread
- etc, etc

I think these noise factors play in all countries and will overwhelm the signal. As such I suspect that time-series models based on the available data at best allow you to do a very short-term extrapolation (days, not weeks) on a country by country basis (for larger countries with largely autonomous states/regions even that may be overreaching). And probably your model will only reflect the inherent noise of the data... (eg counts are lower on Monday, simply because weekend delays, not because of real decrease... given you can at best extrapolate a week that tells you absolutely nothing new or useful).

But I may be wrong in this of course, it is my first experience of this whole Covid19 phenomenon 😉
Agreed.

Two questions here one substantive the other technical.
1) Wouldn't the whole analysis make (even) more sense when using reported death figures instead of cases? Reported deaths seem to be more reliable than reported cases. And they do not suffer from distortions due to changes in size and kind of population tested

2) You smoothed with loess. Doesn't this introduce spurious edge/border effects? Especially at the arguably most interesting part of the curve the right hand side (i.e. now)? I guess you should see differences depending on using first order or second order polynomials for the loess smoother. It seems to me a smoother which just relies on the past would be more appropriate.

So might be ETS or something like that be a better candidate for the smoothing/trend extraction?

1. While the death figures are probably more reliable, as I explained in the post, the log ratios cancel out the problematic issues such as under-reporting, level of testing, etc.
2. No. loess removes the noise and it is particularly suitable as it has good bias properties at the edges. ETS is roughly equivalent but the smoothing parameters are not tuned for smoothing but for forecasting.
